An execution mode governs when the robot requests a new action chunk and how it acts while waiting, creating a fundamental trade-off between robot idle time, observation staleness, and inference frequency. Across the three modes, K K denotes the number of predicted actions per chunk, H H the number executed per chunk, the execution horizon, and L L the inference latency expressed as a number of control steps (§ 3.6 ). Mode 1: Synchronous execution. Synchronous execution is a common deployment pattern in which inference and robot action execution interleaves ( Black et al., 2025c ) . After executing H H actions, the robot requests a new chunk and pauses for L L control steps while inference completes, holding its position and last gripper command. Once the action chunk becomes available, the robot resumes execution from its first predicted action. Pros and cons. Its advantage is its low inference request rate: one request every H + L H+L control steps. Its disadvantage is that the robot pauses during every inference call, which can disrupt tasks that require continuous motion. Idle time. We quantify robot pauses using idle time ( I I ), the number of control steps spent waiting for inference per H H executed actions. Synchronous execution incurs I = L I=L idle steps per execution horizon (hatched in Figure 5 ). Once the first action chunk is available, both asynchronous modes introduced below eliminate pauses ( I = 0 I=0 ), provided the available actions cover the next inference interval. Mode 2: Lazy asynchronous execution. Asynchronous execution avoids robot pauses by running inference while the robot executes actions from an earlier chunk. Lazy execution requests inference least frequently among various asynchronous schedules, starting the next call only when L L of the H H scheduled actions remain so that the next chunk becomes available as the current execution horizon ends. When the new chunk arrives, the robot skips its first L L actions, which correspond to the elapsed inference interval, and executes the following H H actions. Pros and cons. Its advantage is that it keeps the robot moving continuously without pauses. Its disadvantages are that (1) more frequent inference does not reduce average observation staleness relative to synchronous execution, and (2) robot motion during inference can introduce additional uncertainty for tasks requiring precise manipulation. Observation staleness. We define observation staleness as the average time elapsed between capturing a visual observation and executing an action generated from it. As illustrated in Figure 5 , synchronous execution runs actions 0 0 through H − 1 H-1 of each chunk, yielding an average staleness of ( H − 1 ) / 2 + L (H-1)/2+L with an inference latency of L L steps. Because lazy asynchronous execution skips the first L L actions, its observation staleness is identically ( H − 1 ) / 2 + L (H-1)/2+L steps. Mode 3: Continuous asynchronous execution. Continuous execution represents the opposite extreme in asynchronous execution, running inference as frequently as possible by starting each new call as soon as the previous one completes, while the robot continues executing previously predicted actions. At each completion, the robot switches to the new chunk, skips its first L L actions, and executes the next L L actions while another inference call runs, yielding an execution horizon of H = L H=L and an average observation staleness of ( 3 ​ L − 1 ) / 2 (3L-1)/2 steps. Pros and cons. Its advantage is more frequent action updates and thus a lower observation staleness than in either of the other modes when latency is shorter than their execution horizon ( L < 5 L<5 ). The average staleness is even lower than in zero-latency synchronous execution with H = 5 H=5 when L = 1 L=1 . Its disadvantages are a higher inference request rate and more frequent transitions between chunks, which can introduce discontinuities in the robot’s actions. 3.6 Latency Injection Mechanism We simulate inference latency by converting it into a number of simulator control steps. For example, at a control frequency of 20 Hz, a latency of 100 ms corresponds to L = 2 L=2 steps: synchronous execution inserts two stationary actions that hold the robot’s position and last gripper command, whereas asynchronous execution continues executing available actions from the previous chunk. We extend each task’s deadline by the number of inference-induced idle steps to preserve its action budget (Appendix B ). 4 Evaluation and Findings In this section, we use VLALagBench to (1) examine how inference latency affects success across tasks, (2) identify the factors leading to accuracy loss, (3) assess the trade-offs between synchronous and asynchronous execution, and (4) compare latency sensitivity across VLA policies. Set-down requires greater precision than the other tasks. 4.2 Latency sensitivity across tasks Q1. How does inference latency affect task success across different manipulation tasks? Finding 1. Inference latency can substantially reduce task success on moving targets, with the extent of degradation depending on both the task nature and target speed. Empirical success curves confirm that latency penalties emerge primarily when targets move and scale differently across tasks. As shown in Figure 6 , an inference latency of 200 ms under synchronous execution changes success on nearly static targets ( 0.001 0.001 m/s) by only a few percentage points across all tasks. On moving targets, however, even moderate inference latency affects tasks differently: at a target speed of 0.1 0.1 m/s, 100 ms of latency nearly halves set-down success, from 71.5% to 40.5% (57% of its zero-latency success rate). In contrast, grasping success declines only from 86.5% to 74.0%, retaining 86% of its zero-latency success rate. We next examine the factors underlying these differences in latency sensitivity across tasks. Q2. What factors determine a task’s sensitivity to latency? Finding 2. A task’s latency sensitivity depends on its requirements for action precision and continuous motion. (2.1) Tasks requiring high spatial precision suffer from stale observations, whereas (2.2) tasks requiring sustained motion suffer from robot pauses. (2.1) Precision. Stale observations make precise manipulation harder because the target moves between image capture and action execution, so the robot may act on a position the target no longer occupies. Figure 7 compares the precision required by different tasks: set-down requires placing the bowl within a narrow 3 cm zone around the plate’s center, whereas release tolerates drops anywhere across a 12.2 cm basket opening. At a target speed of 0.1 0.1 m/s, 200 ms of additional observation staleness allows the plate to move 2 cm, a displacement equal to two-thirds of set-down ’s tolerance for placement error, making precise placement more difficult. (2.2) Continuous motion. Robot pauses disrupt tasks that require continuous motion, making it harder to catch up with or move alongside the target. Because VLA policies are trained via imitation learning on static demonstrations ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , they issue actions at a nearly constant velocity regardless of how fast the target moves (Figure 11 , Appendix B ). Synchronous execution halts the arm after every H H actions, reducing π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ’s average approach speed by 34% at 200 ms latency during release . This reduced speed causes the arm to fall behind the moving basket before releasing, and prevents the gripper from keeping pace with the moving drawer during articulated-object manipulation . As we quantify in § 5.1 , grasping is more sensitive to observation staleness, articulated manipulation and release are more sensitive to robot pauses, while set-down is sensitive to both. What are the trade-offs between synchronous and asynchronous execution as inference latency increases? Finding 3. Asynchronous execution may recover task success by reducing robot pauses and observation staleness, at the cost of more frequent inference (§ 3.5 ). (3.2) At short inference latencies, continuous asynchronous mode updates actions more frequently, helping tasks that require precise manipulation, such as set-down . (3.1) Removing pauses. In particular, synchronous and lazy asynchronous execution have the same average observation staleness at the same inference latency (§ 3.5 ), so the recovery under lazy execution indicates that removing pauses accounts for much of the improvement. We quantify these policy-specific sensitivities in § 5.1 . 5 System-Specific Configuration Selection with VLALagBench In this section, we build on the preceding findings to guide VLA configuration selection for a given inference system. Specifically, we develop an empirical model that uses limited calibration data for each policy–task pair to predict task success across inference latencies, execution modes, and execution horizons (§ 5.1 ). This model reuses measurements collected on one system to select configurations that maximize predicted task success on a new system (§ 5.2 ). 5.1 An Empirical Model for Task Success Prediction Success model intuition. Stale observations and robot pauses caused by inference latency can make a task harder, much like increasing the target’s speed. This similarity suggests a way to reuse past success measurements: we first measure how task success varies with target speed under one latency and execution mode. To estimate success under another latency and execution modes, we simply look up the success rate on the measured curve at a target speed adjusted for observation staleness and robot idle time.
